summary.text: 我 is used for first-person self-reference. Early forms are interpreted as pictures of a long-handled, toothed implement, though its exact identity is disputed. The picture was probably reused to write the pronoun because of sound; the implement’s spoken name is unknown, so that sound match cannot be confirmed.

formation.text: Pictographic: the graph depicts one toothed, long-handled implement. Its use for the pronoun is a probable borrowing of the whole sign, not a change from “implement” to “I.” No part is established as a phonetic component. The selected oracle-script and bronze-script forms are separate modern redrawings, not proof of a sequence of graphic change.

components.text: The whole graph is interpreted as a long-handled, toothed implement, variously identified as a saw-like tool, an axe-like or ritual weapon, or another object. Its identity is disputed, and the graph is treated here as one picture rather than as separately established parts. A later analysis of the seal form as 戈 plus 𠄒 is uncertain and does not establish the early graph’s components.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze forms are described as implement-like. Early inscriptions also use the graph for first-person reference, as well as for diviner names and a state name. These uses do not establish a chronology or a semantic path between them. The selected oracle-script and bronze-script images are modern redrawings of separately cited examples, not successive stages.

The received Shuowen account defines 我 as self-designation and analyzes its seal form as 戈 plus 𠄒. Later commentary leaves 𠄒 uncertain, including whether it represents 垂 or 殺 and whether it might be phonetic. This analysis does not settle the early graph’s composition.

Graphic variants including 𢦐 are recorded, but the available accounts do not establish a detailed, individually dated path from early scripts to the standard form or support specific claims of graphic corruption.

uncertainties.text: The implement’s identity and spoken name are unsettled. Reusing its picture for the pronoun because the words sounded alike is probable, but the proposed sound match cannot be demonstrated. Reconstructions of the pronoun do not establish the implement’s name.
One oracle-bone example is interpreted as plural self-reference, but the number scope of early uses is unsettled.
No continuous, individually dated sequence of graphic development is established. The later Shuowen component analysis cannot be projected back onto the early picture.

developments.text: The likely account is that the implement picture was reused to write the first-person pronoun because the words sounded alike; the meaning “implement” did not develop into “I.” Early pronoun use is reported, but the implement’s spoken name is unknown, so the sound match cannot be demonstrated.

limitations.text: Diviner-name and state-name uses are reported alongside pronoun uses, but their chronology and any semantic connection are not established.
Early number scope and the chronology of number meanings remain unresolved; one cited oracle example is interpreted as plural self-reference.
